title: OnCo weekly, 2026-11-17
summary: 1555 changelog entries, 5 regulatory events, 2 upcoming dates, 1835 corrections

sections.title: What changed this week
sections.blurb: New pages, new data and fixes, from the changelog.
items: 17 November 2026: Second accuracy pass on 104 care protocols, the emergencies, immunotherapy side effects, cell therapy and everything with drug doses first: 413 wrong and 1,623 overstated claims corrected against the guidelines and labels, among them the fluoropyrimidine dose table for DPYD carriers, the vaccine advice for patients, and steroid doses for a CAR-T side effect; newer guideline editions noted or built in

17 November 2026: Fourteen more care protocols, for side effects that had none: high blood pressure and protein in the urine on VEGF drugs, heart rhythm changes, bleeding on BTK inhibitors, raised liver enzymes, lung inflammation on antibody-drug conjugates, fluid retention, high blood sugar, low magnesium, high phosphate, thyroid changes, differentiation syndrome, capillary leak, tumour flare and constipation; 226 protocols in all

17 November 2026: Second accuracy pass on the original 39 country pages, among them the United States, China, India, Japan, Germany, Brazil and the United Kingdom: about 660 claims corrected after each was read against its source again

17 November 2026: Second accuracy pass on live country pages, last batch for waves 5 to 12: corrections to Austria, Serbia, Denmark, Finland, Norway, Ireland, Hungary, Belarus, Bulgaria and North Korea, each claim read against its source again

17 November 2026: Second accuracy pass on live country pages, continued: corrections to eighteen more pages, among them Haiti, Senegal, Slovenia, Mali, Papua New Guinea, Burkina Faso, Costa Rica, Paraguay, Belgium, Cuba, Czechia, Greece and Portugal, each claim read against its source again

17 November 2026: Second accuracy pass on live country pages: corrections to 53 pages after every claim was read against its source again, including what the IAEA radiotherapy directory lists for 36 countries, WHO's HPV vaccination data where pages had said there was none, and sources pages had called unreadable that do answer

17 November 2026: The first weekly gap fill read from FDA sources lands, each fact checked against the FDA list and device records: the Guardant360 Liquid CDx blood test approved on 19 May 2026 with its seven drug pairings, and four companion tests linked to the biomarkers they read

17 November 2026: More of the graph is joined up: 1,251 confirmed links between people and the trials whose papers they wrote, matched by ORCID or full name and affiliation; who pays for 21 tests in the US and UK, from Medicare national coverage decisions and NICE guidance; fifty warning-card lines now name the protocol that manages them; and eight wrong side-effect links are removed

17 November 2026: Twenty-two more care protocols close the gaps in the census, among them stoma care, drain care at home, transplant conditioning, veno-occlusive disease, lung biopsy, intrathecal chemotherapy in children, end-of-life care for children, advance care planning and stopping smoking after a diagnosis; 212 protocols in all, with a table of what is covered and what is still open

17 November 2026: Shasqi in depth: its clinical programme SQ3370, its trial and the click-activated chemistry behind it, from the company's own pages, the registry and the published papers; the weekly gap-fill job gets the tools it needs to read its allowed sources; and the command-line tool and MCP server are rebuilt to know about care protocols

17 November 2026: A contributor's education work arrives, 215 new records on biomarkers, immune tests, specimens, RNA and clinical evidence, with every source checked; and a backlog of corrections lands: new FDA approvals including pimicotinib, four generic icons removed from logos, mislabelled trials fixed, radiotherapy counts for Madagascar and Angola, the two Cuban lung cancer vaccines, and 33 records renamed for their subject

sections.title: Corrections, past 7 days
sections.blurb: Confirmed factual corrections to the corpus, with the fixing commit.
items: 2026-11-16 · Hypercalcaemia of malignancy: best-supported version: The page said both sources start with assessment and intravenous saline. The Endocrine Society 2023 abstract, the only part of that guideline read, covers drug treatment and does not mention fluids. (Second accuracy pass; Endocrine Society 2023 abstract, read raw from the Europe PMC REST API) · Saline and assessment are now attributed to the Society for Endocrinology 2016 guidance alone.

2026-11-16 · Hypercalcaemia of malignancy: medicines review step: The step told the reader to stop medicines that raise calcium and named calcium and vitamin D supplements. The Society for Endocrinology guidance says only to take a history of drugs including supplements and over-the-counter preparations, and lists thiazide diuretics, lithium, hypervitaminosis D and A and theophylline toxicity among the causes. (Second accuracy pass; Society for Endocrinology 2016 full text XML from Europe PMC (PMC5314807)) · The step now says to ask about all medicines and gives the source's own list of causes. The missing instruction is named in the gaps.

2026-11-16 · Hypercalcaemia of malignancy: bisphosphonate step: The step and summary said to give the bisphosphonate at a lower dose in kidney impairment and presented it as the routine next step. The source says to consider intravenous bisphosphonates if further treatment is required after saline, and to give more slowly and consider dose reduction in renal impairment. (Second accuracy pass; Society for Endocrinology 2016 full text XML from Europe PMC (PMC5314807)) · Reworded to the source's conditions, with the pamidronate and ibandronic acid doses and the pamidronate rate of 20 mg an hour added and quoted.

2026-11-16 · Hypercalcaemia of malignancy: glucocorticoid step and its grade: The page said to add a bisphosphonate or denosumab if calcium stays high or for persistent severe hypercalcaemia. The Endocrine Society says where patients continue to have severe or symptomatic hypercalcaemia. The page also described steroids as for lymphoma and other calcitriol-driven causes, where the Society for Endocrinology lists them second line in lymphoma, other granulomatous diseases or vitamin D poisoning. (Second accuracy pass; Endocrine Society 2023 abstract and Society for Endocrinology 2016 full text, both read raw from Europe PMC) · Step, summary and grade claim reworded to the sources' conditions.

2026-11-16 · Hypercalcaemia of malignancy: certainty ratings: Low certainty was printed against the recommendations on tumours with high calcitriol and on parathyroid carcinoma. The abstract states low certainty in a sentence directly before the three recommendations on denosumab and calcitonin and does not rate the later two separately. (Second accuracy pass; Endocrine Society 2023 abstract, read raw from the Europe PMC REST API; the full text returned 403) · Those two are now given as conditional recommendations without a certainty rating, and the gap is stated.

2026-11-16 · Hypercalcaemia of malignancy: reasons given for steps: Several reasons were not in either source: that calcitonin works within hours, that loop diuretics worsen dehydration, that bisphosphonates damage the kidneys if given too fast, that low albumin hides a high calcium, and that a low PTH points to the cancer, where the source says malignancy or other less common causes. Tiredness and drowsiness were listed as symptoms and are not in the source's list. (Second accuracy pass; Society for Endocrinology 2016 full text XML and Endocrine Society 2023 abstract, both from Europe PMC) · Each reason now says only what the cited source says. The symptoms follow the source's list.

2026-11-16 · Metastatic spinal cord compression: who is immobilised: The page said to immobilise anyone with suspected cord compression and neurological signs or signs of spinal instability, lying flat. NICE says to immobilise people with suspected or confirmed cord compression whose neurological symptoms or signs suggest spinal instability, nursed supine, flat or with partial elevation. (Second accuracy pass; NICE NG234 recommendations 1.4.1 and 1.4.3, fetched and read as raw text) · The step, the summary and the best-in-class statement now give the NICE scope and position.

2026-11-16 · Metastatic spinal cord compression: the 24-hour coordinator: The summary said the coordinator service must be covered 24 hours a day. NICE says services should ensure the role is covered 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
